An origin is REQUIRED rather than optional, because an optional one is the one a caller forgets on the path that matters. scripts/s32-origin-test.ts, 10 assertions. Sabotaged five ways: drop the origin from the citation (1 red - it cited as a filename), also write a memory (1 red), make the origin optional (1 red), stamp the run's url on every page (1 red), keep no snapshots (2 red). TWO OF THOSE SABOTAGES CRASHED THE SUITE PARTWAY AND LEFT A FIXTURE PROJECT BEHIND, one of them after writing a memory_item - because teardown sat after the last assertion and never ran. That is not untidiness: Stage B routing re-homes an inbox event into a matching project, so a leftover fixture is a live routing target, and it has already cost this project most of an evening once. clear-test-litter removed them, teardown moved into a finally, and the fix was verified by re-running a CRASHING sabotage and confirming nothing was left. s17-artifacts-test is red in this worktree for the usual reason - no sibling console checkout, and it fails before any assertion - and although this change does touch the artifacts table, the citation suites that actually exercise it (s30-citation, s30-retrieval, s30-restore) all pass.

steps.title: Notification policy
steps.evidence: WHATSAPP NOW HAS THE CLOSED LIST THE PHONE ALREADY HAD. The plan's diagnosis is that everything in section 17 governs REPLIES - he asked, Jarvis answers - while the message Jarvis sends when he did not ask for anything was ungoverned, and the sources kept accumulating: weekly findings, a proposed capability, an auth handoff, an approval, a maintenance issue, a queued desktop action. 'Each one is defensible on its own, and together they turn the pager into a feed.' src/unprompted.ts is S23's shape applied to the channel that had none: eight reasons, enforced at the send site, everything else refused. THE OVERRIDE IS S23'S OBJECT, IMPORTED, NOT A SECOND ONE - the plan's reason is one sentence worth keeping, 'two override lists diverge and the looser one wins', so an unprompted reason carries no override flag of its own; it names which of S23's six it corresponds to and overrides exactly when that one does. Adding a WhatsApp reason that rings through the night therefore requires editing the list the phone reads. Quiet hours HOLD rather than drop, with the row written immediately so the console is accurate at 06:00 if he looks - which closes the routing bug the plan names, where S23 blocks a call at 03:00 and the call becomes a WhatsApp, so the rule that stops the phone ringing routes the interruption to the same phone by another route. Three items in a window become one message with three lines, each link on its own line, because a message with three items and one link at the bottom sends him to the wrong page two times in three. A refused reason is RECORDED as refused rather than dropped, since a caller that ignores the return value would otherwise make it invisible, and 'how often did something want to message him' is the question that catches a feed forming. scripts/s33-unprompted-test.ts, 19 assertions, with the absence asserted the way the plan demands: ten plausible unlisted reasons - task_finished, build_green, deploy_succeeded, daily_digest and six more, each of which a future feature would reasonably want - are all refused, because 'a test that only proves the six work would pass on a system that also sends nine others'. Sabotaged six ways: open the list (5 red), give a blocker the override too (5 red), make quiet hours never apply (5 red), send each item separately (3 red), drain refused rows (1 red), and silence replies during quiet hours. THAT LAST ONE PASSED AT FIRST AND SHOULD NOT HAVE. My assertion called mayReply() with no argument, so it tested whatever time the suite happened to run at - 14:00 - and a version obeying quiet hours was green. The plan's requirement is specifically 'he messages at 02:00, Jarvis replies at 02:00', so mayReply now ACCEPTS a clock and ignores it: ignored because the answer does not depend on the hour, which is the rule, and accepted because a rule about 02:00 has to be testable at 02:00. AND A PROCESS MISTAKE I MADE TWICE NOW: the sabotage script ends with git checkout on src/, which reverted that very fix because I had made the source edit and run the sabotage in one command. The suite still passed, because JavaScript ignores extra arguments, so the hole reopened silently under a commit message claiming it was fixed. Caught by checking git status rather than by the suite. Commit the fix, then sabotage - the same lesson as the S30 replacement tick, and the second time it has cost me a cycle. NOT BUILT for S33: the weekly report itself (S38 renders it as a document plus two lines), the staleness classes (wait / re-raise / block) and their fortnight behaviour, and Needs You sorting oldest first with a re-raised Issue saying what changed. AN ISSUE NOW CARRIES A STALENESS POLICY, AND THE THREE CLASSES ARE THREE BEHAVIOURS. The plan names the gap precisely: Jarvis raises an Issue, sends one message and then by design says nothing more, and 'the plan never says what happens if he does not act'. S46's 'it stays parked and does not nag' is right for an auth handoff and, written as a general principle, is wrong - 'because the first implementation will apply it to everything, including the backup that has been failing for a month'. Migration 054 and src/staleness.ts. THE DISTINCTION IS NOT IMPORTANCE, IT IS WHETHER WAITING COSTS ANYTHING: wait when nothing degrades while he decides, re-raise when it costs more every day, block when waiting is not acceptable at all. Written as a TABLE rather than inferred from severity, because severity answers 'how bad' and this answers 'does waiting make it worse', and they come apart constantly - setup.pending is high severity and still waits. The suite asserts that directly: two high-severity categories land in different classes, so the policy is not severity wearing a hat. AN UNCLASSIFIED CATEGORY DEFAULTS TO re-raise, and the choice is the argument: defaulting to wait is exactly the failure the plan describes in one sentence, the backup silent for a month because nobody wrote a row for it; defaulting to block would stop the system over a category somebody forgot to fill in. Noisy once a week and stopping nothing is the right cost for 'we do not know yet'. RE-RAISING GOES IN THE WEEKLY REPORT AND NOWHERE ELSE - 'a second notification channel for old news is how the pager becomes a feed, and S33's closed list would have to grow, which it should not' - so nothing in this module sends anything; it produces the lines the report carries, and weekly_report is already on that list. A re-raised line carries the age and the count and says what CHANGED: 'open 14 days, since 20 Aug, 13 occurrences, 4 more times since you last saw it', because the sentence he already ignored is not the sentence he should get next. Needs You sorts oldest first, since 'the oldest unresolved item is by definition the one being ignored, and putting it last is how it stays that way'. scripts/s33-staleness-test.ts, 16 assertions, and the central one compares the three classes AGAINST EACH OTHER rather than checking them one at a time: three distinct (in-report, blocking) pairs is what 'three behaviours' means, and a suite asserting them separately would pass on a system where all three did both - which is the failure the plan is describing. Sabotaged five ways: default to wait (2 red), put every class in the report (3 red, including the three-behaviours assertion), move a wait category to re-raise so the classes track severity (4 red), repeat the same sentence on a re-raise (4 red), sort Needs You newest first (2 red). NOT BUILT for S33: the weekly report itself, which S38 renders as a document plus two lines rather than a message.

steps.title: Schedules, maintenance, improvement
steps.evidence: THE SELF-REPAIR NO LONGER HAS DELETING HIS DATA AS ITS CHEAPEST LEVER. The plan's own heading, and the reason it needed one: N7 is 'disk hits 85 percent at 03:00, Maintenance prunes images and old artifacts, and does not wake him' - but ARTIFACTS ARE THE CORPUS S30 ANSWERS FROM, so the automatic remedy for a full disk, running unattended at three in the morning, is deleting the thing he will ask about next month. And 'it would not even fail visibly: S30's test dumps documents and asks three weeks later, and it passes on the day it is written. The failure arrives in production, as an honest I do not have that about something he definitely gave Jarvis.' src/maintenance.ts is built as an ALLOW-LIST of what may be reclaimed rather than a deny-list of what must be kept, and the difference decides the failure mode: a deny-list that forgets a category deletes it, and a category nobody thought of is exactly what the next kind of artifact will be. Everything unlisted is data. Two justifications only - REBUILDABLE (images, caches, reaped worktrees) or EXPIRED (audio past its 7/10 day retention, compacted events) - and an entry that is neither does not belong there whatever it would free. Refusals are RETURNED with their reason rather than silently dropped, so a future caller adding a category sees the word no. When the allow-list is exhausted and the disk is still climbing it raises an Issue rather than pruning deeper, in the re-raise class from IV.2, saying 'I cannot free more without deleting things you asked me to keep' and handing the decision back: 'that is his decision, not a 3am one'. INGEST DEGRADES BEFORE IT DELETES - above the threshold a new upload is refused with a truthful reason rather than accepted and quietly pruned later, because refusing is recoverable and accepting-then-deleting is not, and it looks like success at the moment it happens. The refusal threshold sits ABOVE the prune threshold so reclaiming is tried first, and the check is on THIS write - a single upload big enough to cross the line is refused before it is written, since a partially written artifact that filled the disk is the shape that takes the box down rather than merely disappointing him. scripts/s34-maintenance-test.ts, 17 assertions, and it is a real end-to-end: a document is dumped through S30's ingest, the disk is forced to 86 percent, Maintenance runs, and the question is asked again through the real retrieval path. The candidate list deliberately OFFERS his artifacts and the corpus, because a suite offering only safe candidates proves nothing about the gate. Sabotaged five ways: replace the allow-list with a deny-list that forgets the corpus (5 red), never raise the Issue (3 red), accept uploads above the threshold (2 red), ignore the size of the incoming write (1 red), wake him (1 red). AND THE FIRST RUN OF THE DENY-LIST SABOTAGE EXPOSED MY OWN TEST: it approved knowledge_chunks for deletion and the document survived anyway, because the fixture's perform callback only RECORDED what it was told to delete. A test whose destructive step is a no-op cannot tell a working gate from a missing one - it was passing on the approval list rather than on the corpus. perform now really deletes, and the same sabotage now fails with 'THE DOCUMENT IS GONE'. NOT BUILT for S34: schedules with overlap and misfire policy, the assertion that exactly one scheduler exists (Jarvis's worker, with no jarvis: automation on the OpenClaw side), and the weekly Improvement scan with capped one-tap approvals and a declined candidate that does not come back. THE ALLOW-LIST FAILED OPEN, AND I FOUND IT BY RE-RUNNING SOMEBODY ELSE'S SWEEP. The Tester's f220c69 closed the reason lists against inherited property names, with a note worth copying: 'found by sweeping for the shape rather than assuming that one was the only one'. maintenance.ts and staleness.ts landed AFTER that sweep, so I ran it over my own modules rather than assuming I was covered, and both were broken. planReclaim tested membership with 'c.kind in RECLAIMABLE', and 'constructor' in any object literal is TRUE, so constructor, toString, __proto__, valueOf and hasOwnProperty were all APPROVED FOR UNATTENDED DELETION - failing OPEN, in the gate I had described one tick earlier as the only thing standing between a 3am prune and his corpus. An allow-list that lets five things through is not one. stalenessFor indexed with '?? DEFAULT', and for an inherited key the index returns something truthy so the fallback never fires: it returned a FUNCTION where the signature promises a Staleness, and that value goes into issues.staleness and its CHECK constraint, turning a classification into a database error at the moment an Issue is being raised about something else. A third, smaller one in unprompted.ts's drain, where the reason comes off a row and '?.label' reads undefined off a function, falling through only by luck of that function not having a label. All three ask the question they meant now, with Object.hasOwn. THE TESTER FOUND THE MAINTENANCE ONE CONCURRENTLY and fixed it on main while I was fixing it here - PR #322, and they observed it against the deployed dist on the box. The rebase conflicted and I kept THEIR comment rather than mine, because 'observed on the box' is better evidence than my reasoning about it locally. staleness.ts and the unprompted drain were still unfixed on main, so those halves stand. Assertions added to both suites naming the five inherited keys explicitly, and sabotaging each lookup back to its original form makes them red. Worth recording about the shape rather than the instances: every one of these is an object literal indexed by a string that came from outside, while the Set and Map versions elsewhere in this code - TOOL_BEARING, ADAPTERS, READ_ONLY_KINDS - were never vulnerable. That is the argument for reaching for a Map when the key is not ours. L14 IS BUILT, AND THE DUPLICATE-FIRE GUARANTEE WAS A CONVENTION RATHER THAN A CONSTRAINT. The worker already keyed idempotency on (schedule_id, scheduled_for) - the right key, and the plan's Debug note says a duplicate fire after a restart means it is keyed on something else - but it enforced that with a SELECT followed by an INSERT, which two workers, or one restarted between the two statements, both walk straight through. Migration 055 adds the unique index and recordRun inserts ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, so the constraint is the guarantee and the check above it is only an optimisation; when the insert loses, the task just created is withdrawn rather than left to run twice. PROVED BY RACING RATHER THAN BY SEQUENCING: asserting that a second call returns 'already ran' only tests the SELECT, so the suite fires two inserts for the same minute simultaneously and asserts exactly one wins - and with the index dropped, both won and two rows existed, which is the bug. The decision moved out of the worker loop into src/schedule.ts as a PURE function, so a box that was off for six hours, a run still in flight, and a schedule two failures deep are a line of test rather than a live rehearsal; what is left in the loop is I/O. A MISSED WINDOW IS MISSED, NOT CAUGHT UP - past the fifteen-minute grace it is skipped with an Issue explaining why, because catching up looks like diligence and is how a box that was off overnight fires eight hours of hourly schedules in one minute, unattended. Overlap is decided by policy rather than by luck of timing: skip drops the window, replace fires and names the run it cancels, parallel and queue fire alongside. Three consecutive failures pause the schedule AND raise an Issue, because 'a schedule that silently stops has usually hit its error count and paused itself - that is correct behaviour, but it must be visible in the console rather than only in a column'. The count is DERIVED from the run history rather than kept in a column, for the same reason as S31's classified hash: a counter has to be reset by whoever succeeds, and the day somebody adds a success path that forgets is the day a healthy schedule stays paused. A skip leaves a row, or a schedule that never runs and one that was never due are the same absence. scripts/s34-schedule-test.ts, 17 assertions. Sabotaged five ways: catch up a missed window (1 red), never pause (1 red), ignore overlap (1 red), count failures cumulatively so a success does not reset (1 red), and drop the unique index (2 red, both inserts accepted). ONE ATTRIBUTION WORTH RECORDING: s11-recovery-test came back 24/2 in the first sweep and I had changed worker.ts, so I treated it as mine - but it passes 26/0 on my branch twice and on main, and s4-recovery-test fails identically on both. The suite starts a worker and waits up to 150 seconds on a queue, so it is timing-sensitive; two runs each way was what separated flakiness from a regression, and guessing either way would have been wrong. NOT BUILT for S34: the weekly Improvement scan with capped one-tap approvals and a declined candidate that does not come back, and the box-side assertion that no jarvis: automation exists on the OpenClaw side. THE IMPROVEMENT SCAN SUGGESTS AND NEVER ACTS. Migration 056 and src/improvement.ts. 'Nothing activates itself' is enforced by the module having no route to do so - recordScan cannot start a task, change a setting or send a message, and approve is the only function that creates anything - and it is ASSERTED AS AN ABSENCE ACROSS A WHOLE SCAN rather than by checking one thing: task count, schedule count and approved count all unchanged over twenty findings, because the interesting version of this bug is a scan that acts on the one category nobody thought to check. A DECLINE IS PINNED TO A FINGERPRINT OF THE PROPOSAL, the same shape S31 uses for a tool's classification and for the same reason: the thing being gated is the thing that would otherwise get to say it had changed. The fingerprint is over what it would DO, not over how it is described - a scan that rewords its pitch has not changed its mind, and bringing a declined suggestion back because the adjectives moved is nagging with extra steps. Asserted directly: a reworded title and pitch with the same proposal stays declined. When the proposal genuinely changes it returns on its own, no un-declining required, and the line says what changed rather than repeating the pitch he already turned down - the same rule as S33's re-raised Issue. A declined candidate's times_seen does NOT climb, so nothing quietly accumulates a case for asking again. The asks are capped at three with the rest on the console, because twenty suggestions is a feed and S33's whole point is that a pager stops being read when it becomes one. Approving produces a QUEUED TASK and links the candidate to it, because 'one-tap approval that produces no work is a button, not a decision', and a second tap produces no second task. scripts/s34-improvement-test.ts, 15 assertions. Sabotaged five ways: let the scan start work (1 red, tasks 177 to 197), remove the cap (1 red), let a declined candidate come back unchanged (7 red), put the wording in the fingerprint so rewording revives a decline (2 red), and make approval a status change with no task (2 red). AND MY TEARDOWN CRASHED ON A FOREIGN KEY THE FIRST TIME: improvement_candidates.approved_task_id points INTO tasks, and I deleted the task first. Because that was the finally block, the refusal threw past the summary and left the entire fixture behind - twenty candidates, a task and a project - which is worse than the ordering mistake itself. The rule the S29 teardown work already paid for: walk the references before the things they point at, and do not assume an order because it reads naturally. Cleared with clear-test-litter and the order fixed. WHAT REMAINS FOR S34 is box-side: the assertion that no jarvis: automation exists on the OpenClaw side to fire a schedule a second time, which needs OpenClaw running and is the Tester's.
